note: Researched recommendations, written in the site's voice but by somebody who has not been. Opinionated on purpose — a list of facts is not a guide — but every card says plainly that it was researched rather than visited, and a handwritten note in notes.json overrules any of it. Written against the holes the generated tiers cannot fill: Wikidata knows of three cafés and two bakeries in the whole Bay Area and no markets at all, and the Peninsula has almost nothing.
rules: Every record needs a source and a lastVerified date. If it cannot be checked, it does not go in.
Say what to order and when to go. 'Lovely atmosphere' helps nobody.
Set touristy: true for anywhere that is a sight rather than a local habit — it stays eligible for Culture and Worth the trip, and drops out of the everyday sections.
quality and uniqueness cap at 4 here. 5 is reserved for somewhere one of you actually loved.
No opening hours in prose. OpenStreetMap carries them, js/hours.js reads them, and a time written here is a time that rots.
Nothing about how good the coffee is unless somebody published a reason. Being famous is not a reason.

items.title: Tartine Bakery
items.hoursFrom: tartinebakery.com — closed only on Thanksgiving and Christmas Day
items.why: The morning bun is the thing to queue for — bready rather than flaky, with marmalade hidden in the middle — and it sells out. Chad Robertson and Elisabeth Prueitt won the Beard for Outstanding Pastry Chef here in 2008, and his 2010 book is the one that started half the world baking sourdough. The fresh bread lands mid-afternoon, so a morning visit and an afternoon one are two different errands.
items.source: James Beard Foundation; SFGate; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: b. patisserie
items.why: Order the kouign-amann and nothing else until you have had one: laminated Breton dough with a layer of sugar that turns to liquid caramel at the base. Belinda Leong won the James Beard award for Outstanding Baker for this shop, and her partner Michel Suas founded the San Francisco Baking Institute, which is to say the city's bakers were taught by him.
items.source: James Beard Foundation; bpatisserie.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Arizmendi Bakery
items.why: A worker-owned cooperative, one of the network the Cheese Board Collective in Berkeley helped start, and they bake exactly one kind of pizza a day — whatever whoever is on shift decided, chalked on the board outside. Sourdough crust, by the slice or the whole pie. Going without checking the board first is the point.
items.source: arizmendibakery.com; Wikipedia; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Good Mong Kok Bakery
items.hoursFrom: openstreetmap; the same on Tripadvisor and Corner
items.why: Cash, no seats, and a queue that moves faster than you will be ready for — you point at what you want through the glass and it goes in a box. Har gow, siu mai, baked char siu bao, roughly a dollar a piece. Decide before you reach the counter. Eat it on the steps of Portsmouth Square.
items.source: The San Francisco Standard; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Ritual Coffee Roasters
items.why: The Valencia Street room that opened in 2005 and is generally credited with starting San Francisco on specialty coffee — it was buying direct from farms by 2006, before that was a thing anyone advertised. Worth knowing which one you are in: this is the original.
items.source: Wikipedia; ritualcoffee.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Andytown Coffee Roasters
items.why: Ask for a Snowy Plover: espresso over sparkling water and ice with brown sugar and whipped cream on top, which sounds wrong and is the reason people come out here. The Irish soda bread is the other one. Two streets from Ocean Beach, so it is a stop on the way rather than a destination — take it with you.
items.source: SF Weekly; andytownsf.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Ferry Plaza Farmers Market
items.why: Saturday is the big one — over a hundred farmers and makers, and the morning most of the city's cooks are there. Tuesday and Thursday are smaller and much easier to actually shop. Run by the non-profit Foodwise, year round, rain or shine.
items.source: foodwise.org; ferrybuildingmarketplace.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Alemany Farmers Market
items.why: California's first farmers market, opened in 1943, and still the one where the produce is cheap and the crowd is people shopping rather than browsing. The city tried to close it in 1946 and was overruled by ballot. Saturdays; the flea market takes the same lot on Sundays.
items.source: foodwise.org; San Francisco Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Swan Oyster Depot
items.hoursFrom: openstreetmap; the same on Tripadvisor and Corner — Swan has no website
items.why: Eighteen stools at a marble counter on Polk Street since 1912, cash only, no reservations, no tables, and it shuts in the early afternoon. Oysters, the crab Louis, the smoked salmon, chowder. Go before eleven or expect to wait an hour on the pavement, and bring notes — the nearest cash machine is across the road.
items.source: SFGate; Tripadvisor listing; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: La Taqueria
items.hoursFrom: lataqueriasf.net, which presents itself as the restaurant’s site
items.why: A James Beard America's Classic, and the burrito people argue about: Miguel Jara leaves the rice out entirely, puts in more meat, and griddles the outside until it is golden. Ask for it dorado. If you have opinions about Mission burritos this is the one they are measured against.
items.source: James Beard Foundation 2017; Mission Local; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Tommaso's Ristorante Italiano
items.why: The first wood-fired brick pizza oven on the West Coast, lit in 1935 by a Neapolitan family who brought the oven with them, and still the oven the pizza comes out of. Alice Waters is said to have modelled the one at Chez Panisse on it. Downstairs, in booths, the way it has always been.
items.source: San Francisco Chronicle; Pizza Hall of Fame; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Green Apple Books
items.why: On Clement Street since 1967, when Richard Savoy opened it at twenty-five with a credit union loan and a stock of second-hand paperbacks. It has grown about tenfold into the building since, new and used shelved together across two floors of small themed rooms. An hour disappears here; budget for it.
items.source: greenapplebooks.com store history; Wikipedia; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Kepler's Books
items.why: Opened in 1955 by Roy Kepler, a conscientious objector who had been interned for it, and it became the Peninsula's counterculture hub — the Grateful Dead played here early on. Still independent, still running a serious events programme. Café Borrone is next door and has been since 1989; the two are one outing, not two.
items.source: keplers.com; Wikipedia; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Zareen's
items.why: Zareen Khan cooks her family's Karachi recipes on California Avenue, and it is the chicken Memoni samosas that got her into the Michelin Guide. Halal, counter service, and the rare Peninsula place that is neither a chain nor an expense account.
items.source: Michelin Guide; The Stanford Daily; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Manresa Bread
items.hoursFrom: manresabread.toast.site — opens daily at 8am, closes at 6pm
items.why: The bakery that grew out of Manresa, the Michelin three-star in Los Gatos. Avery Ruzicka mills the grain in house — rye, red and white wheat — which is why the bread tastes of something rather than of nothing. The Peninsula has one bakery of this order and this is it.
items.source: San Francisco Chronicle; manresabread.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Lake Merced Park
items.why: Four and a half miles of flat paved path all the way round the lake, past the rowing clubs and through eucalyptus, with about 130 feet of climb in the whole loop. It is the run in San Francisco that asks nothing of your legs — an hour and a half at a walk, well under that running, and no junctions to stop at.
items.source: AllTrails; TrailLink; SFGate; existence and position confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.hoursFrom: San Francisco Park Code §3.21 — city parks close from midnight to 5am

items.title: Coupa Café
items.why: Order an arepa and a Venezuelan hot chocolate, which is spiced and not sweet. Nancy Coupal lived in Caracas for twenty-seven years and opened this in 2004 to be near her children at Stanford. The Coupa kiosks on campus came later, from this shop. Go to the Ramona original, a 1930s building, rather than the newer Lytton branch by the station.
items.source: Palo Alto Online (twenty years, 2024); coupacafe.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.coordsFrom: osm, Coupa Cafe at 538 Ramona Street — the record had matched the campus kiosk on Via Ortega

items.title: Oklava
items.why: A Turkish family bakery whose name means the rolling pin that baklava is made with. The case holds around twenty kinds, so buy a mixed box of pistachio, walnut and hazelnut rather than one slice of the classic. It also does a proper Turkish breakfast. And it stays open late enough to be somewhere to go after dinner on University.
items.source: Verde Magazine; Punch Magazine; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Palo Alto Farmer's Market
items.hoursFrom: pafarmersmarket.org — every Saturday, with a short break over the holidays
items.why: Palo Alto's oldest farmers' market, on Gilman Street every Saturday since 1983. It is a small one — fruit, bread, cheese, eggs, fish and flowers — and it is run by volunteers who give the proceeds to Avenidas, the town's senior centre. Go early, before the good stone fruit is gone, and walk to University for coffee afterwards.
items.source: pafarmersmarket.org; Punch Magazine; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Palo Alto Creamery
items.why: A 1950s diner on Emerson and Hamilton, from a family dairy business that started here in 1923. Sit at the counter for a milkshake, and have a slice of pie, which the old Creamery fountain was famous for. It suits a weekend brunch with children, or anyone who is tired of small plates.
items.source: Verde Magazine (centennial); Nob Hill Gazette; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Ramen Nagi
items.why: The first American branch of a Tokyo ramen shop, opened on Bryant Street in 2018. You tick boxes on a card for broth richness, noodle firmness, garlic and spice. Get the Original King, a pork-bone tonkotsu, and ask for the noodles firm. The queue is the price. Arrive before it opens or late in the afternoon, never at seven.
items.source: The Infatuation; Ramen Club; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Tane Vegan Izakaya
items.why: A small Japanese izakaya where everything is plant-based and nothing tastes like a compromise. The rolls are the point: order the Point Reyes, made with king oyster mushroom, and the Ewa, with enoki tempura and matcha salt. There are very few tables, so book even on a weeknight.
items.source: HappyCow; trybayarea.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Bistro Maxine
items.hoursFrom: openstreetmap; the same on Tripadvisor and Yelp
items.why: A crêperie on Ramona, open since 2006, that began as the smallest restaurant in Palo Alto with a liquor licence. Order a savoury galette, then the crêpe Suzette, which is flambéed. The sidewalk tables are the closest thing downtown has to a Paris café.
items.source: bistromaxine.com; OpenTable; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Scoop Microcreamery
items.why: Small-batch ice cream frozen to order with liquid nitrogen, so it comes out denser than churned. The owners are home bakers, and the flavours show it: salted caramel with bourbon vanilla, or Biscoff and cream. It is the place for dessert after dinner on University.
items.source: The Stanford Daily (April 2026); Palo Alto Online; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Blue Bottle Coffee
items.why: Order the New Orleans iced coffee: cold-brewed with roasted chicory and cut with milk and a little sugar. James Freeman first sold it at Bay Area farmers' markets in 2005, before Blue Bottle had cafés. There is a second branch at Stanford Shopping Center, but this is the one on University.
items.source: bluebottlecoffee.com; LAist; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.coordsFrom: osm, Blue Bottle Coffee at 525 University Avenue, where the café now is

items.title: Gamble Garden
items.why: Two and a half acres around a 1902 house in Old Palo Alto: a rose garden, a wisteria garden, an herb garden and an allée. It was left to the city by the granddaughter of Procter & Gamble's co-founder. It is free and open every day during daylight, and it is rarely busy — somewhere to sit rather than somewhere to see.
items.source: gamblegarden.org; SFGate; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Rodin Sculpture Garden
items.why: Twenty Rodin bronzes in the open air beside the Cantor, including a full cast of The Gates of Hell. Stanford's Rodin collection is the largest outside Paris. It is free and never closes. Docents give free tours on Wednesday afternoons and at weekends, and the Cantor next door is free too.
items.source: The Stanford Daily; Cantor Arts Center; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.hoursFrom: museum.stanford.edu — open all day, every day, since 1985

items.title: Baylands Nature Preserve
items.hoursFrom: paloalto.gov — open space hours, 8am to sunset; the interpretive centre itself opens Sa 12–3, Su 10–3

match.name: Lucy Evans Baylands Nature Interpretive Center

items.why: Salt marsh at the edge of the Bay, and one of the best places to watch birds on the West Coast. A boardwalk runs a quarter of a mile from this centre across the marsh to open water. Autumn to spring is the season: shorebirds and ducks stop here on the Pacific Flyway. For photographs, early mornings from March to May.
items.source: KQED; Santa Clara Valley Bird Alliance; Wikipedia; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Pacific Art League
items.why: Downtown's art school, in a historic building on Ramona: over fifty classes a term in watercolour, oil and acrylic, drawing, life drawing, sculpture and photography, taught by working artists. It runs quarterly terms plus one-off weekend workshops, and a workshop is the easy way to find out whether you want the term.
items.source: pacificartleague.org; Wikipedia; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: The Penny Ice Creamery
items.why: Small-batch ice cream from Santa Cruz, made from scratch in the shop with organic dairy. It is one of the smallest dairy plants in California, and you can watch it being churned. The flavours follow the season, and the torched marshmallow topping is the one people queue for. It is in Town & Country, across El Camino from Stanford.
items.source: thepennyicecreamery.com; Verde Magazine; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Rick's Ice Cream
items.why: Palo Alto's old ice cream shop: about seventy years on Middlefield at Charleston, with four dozen flavours made on site. Try Computer Chip, which is chocolate with chocolate chips and orange zest, or the kulfi, or Blue Moon. The Pints of Joy team took it over this year and added black sesame and Alphonso mango without retiring the old ones.
items.source: Palo Alto Online (January 2026); ricksicecream.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Marvel Cake
items.why: A small patisserie on University doing French technique with Asian flavours. The mango crêpe cake, thin crêpes layered with cream and mango, is the thing to order. Good coffee too, and a few seats.
items.source: Yelp; Wanderlog; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.hoursFrom: the joe coffee listing; Yelp agrees

items.title: SusieCakes
items.why: An old-fashioned American cake shop on Santa Cruz Avenue. The six-layer chocolate cake is the signature, with the red velvet close behind. Buy it by the slice for today, or order a whole one for a birthday.
items.source: susiecakes.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Caffe Trieste
items.why: The first espresso house on the West Coast. Giovanni Giotta opened it in 1956 because he missed the coffee of Trieste. It became the Beats' café, with Kerouac and Ferlinghetti, and Francis Ford Coppola wrote much of The Godfather screenplay at a table in the corner. Order a cappuccino and sit. It is about the room more than the cup.
items.source: Wikipedia; caffetrieste.com; 7x7; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Sightglass Coffee
items.hoursFrom: openstreetmap; the same on Tripadvisor and SF Station
items.why: The Morrison brothers' flagship: a roastery in a big SoMa warehouse on 7th Street, open since 2010. They started with a coffee cart the year before. The roaster works in the middle of the room, and there is a loft with seating above the bar, which makes it one of the few serious coffee rooms where you can stay and work.
items.source: sightglasscoffee.com; Food GPS; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Four Barrel Coffee
items.why: One of the roasters that started San Francisco’s specialty coffee movement, on Valencia since 2008. Walk it together with Ritual, a few blocks up the same street, and taste the two side by side.
items.source: Wikipedia; fourbarrelcoffee.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: The Coffee Movement
items.why: A tiny standing-room shop on Washington Street, between Chinatown and Nob Hill. It is one of the city's most talked-about coffee counters. Order the tasting flight: three of the day's coffees, brewed different ways side by side. It isn't somewhere to stay with a laptop. Have one very good cup, talk to the baristas, and walk on.
items.source: Eater SF (January 2026); Food & Wine; Filter Notes; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Kopi Kita
items.why: San Francisco's first Indonesian coffee shop, on Lombard, which opened as Kopiku and is now Kopi Kita. The beans come from small Indonesian farms through the owners' own roastery, Beaneka. Order the pandan latte, which is just sweet and tastes faintly of vanilla. The avocado coffee is the adventurous one. Pineapple tarts go with either.
items.source: San Francisco Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Turtle Tower
items.why: The best Northern-style pho in the city: the Hanoi way, with a clear, gingery broth and none of the hoisin and basil on the side. Order the pho ga, made with free-range chicken and skin-on strips of meat. It was a Tenderloin fixture from 1999, closed in 2023, and came back on California Street. A second branch is on Fillmore in Cow Hollow.
items.source: The Infatuation; SF Standard; SFGate; moved from its old address on Larkin Street, where the map still has it

items.title: Liguria Bakery
items.why: Focaccia and nothing else, baked by the same family on Washington Square since 1911. Plain, onion, garlic, pizza-style with tomato — wrapped in white paper and handed over the counter. It opens early and closes when the trays are empty, often before noon, so this is a morning errand.
items.source: SF Chronicle; SF Eater; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.hoursNote: Tuesday to Saturday from 7, until the focaccia runs out — often before noon.

items.title: Victoria Pastry Company
items.why: An Italian pastry shop since 1914 — cannoli filled to order, zuccotto, and the St. Honoré cake that North Beach birthdays are built around. Old-school in the good way: the case is the menu.
items.source: victoriapastry.com; SF Eater; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Golden Gate Bakery
items.why: The Chinatown egg tart, still warm, custard barely set inside a flaky lard crust. Famous for closing without warning for weeks at a time — if the shutter is up and there is a queue, join it.
items.source: SF Chronicle; SF Eater; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.hoursNote: Posted hours are daily 8 to 8, but it keeps irregular hours and sometimes closes for weeks — check before you go.

items.title: Stella Pastry
items.why: Home of the sacripantina, a sponge-and-zabaglione cake made here since the 1940s and hard to find anywhere else. Buy a slice and a cannoli and eat them standing on Columbus.
items.source: SF Eater; SFGate; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Réveille Coffee Co.
items.why: The North Beach café for people who care what the coffee is — roasted by Réveille themselves, pulled carefully, in a small flatiron-ish room where Columbus meets Grant. A good counterweight to the neighbourhood's old espresso bars.
items.source: reveillecoffee.com; SF Eater; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Caffè Greco
items.why: A Columbus Avenue espresso bar in the Trieste tradition: marble tables, a proper cappuccino, affogato in the afternoon, and a window seat for watching North Beach go by.
items.source: SFGate; Yelp; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Mario's Bohemian Cigar Store Cafe
items.why: Nobody sells cigars here any more. A narrow bar on the corner of Washington Square doing focaccia sandwiches — the meatball is the classic — with a glass of wine or a coffee, and the park through the window.
items.source: SF Chronicle; SFGate; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Red Blossom Tea Company
items.why: A family tea shop on Grant since 1985, run now by the second generation. They will brew you a tasting of oolongs or pu-erh at the counter and explain each one — the most useful half hour in Chinatown for anyone curious about tea.
items.source: redblossomtea.com; SF Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Molinari Delicatessen
items.why: An Italian deli on Columbus since 1896. Take a number, order a sandwich on a sweet roll — the 'Joe's Special' or a hot coppa — and eat it in Washington Square. The salami is made to their own recipe.
items.source: molinarisalame.com; SF Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Tony's Pizza Napoletana
items.why: Tony Gemignani's pizzeria, which does twelve styles from twelve ovens. The Margherita he won the Naples world championship with is capped at 73 a day — ask for it when you sit down.
items.source: tonyspizzanapoletana.com; SF Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Sotto Mare
items.why: A loud, cramped oyster bar with the best cioppino in the city — the crab-heavy, tomato-rich San Francisco stew, served in a pot with a bib. Go early; no reservations.
items.source: SF Chronicle; SF Eater; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Z & Y Restaurant
items.why: Serious Sichuan in Chinatown — chilli-heaped fried chicken, fish in fire-red broth, dan dan noodles. A Michelin Bib Gourmand for years; expect a queue at weekends.
items.source: Michelin Guide (Bib Gourmand); SF Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Red Rock Coffee
items.why: The living room of downtown Mountain View — a big two-storey coffeehouse at the top of Castro Street, run as a community place with open-mic nights. Good espresso and room to sit for an afternoon.
items.source: redrockcoffee.org; Mountain View Voice; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Dana Street Roasting Company
items.why: Mountain View's own roaster, on Dana Street since the 1990s. Unpretentious, with the beans roasted on site; the house espresso is worth the half-block detour off Castro.
items.source: danastreetroasting.com; Mountain View Voice; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Maison Alyzée
items.why: A small French pâtisserie on Castro Street — croissants, kouign-amann and fruit tarts made in the back. The Mountain View answer to a Paris morning.
items.source: maisonalyzee.com; Yelp; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Alexander's Patisserie
items.why: The pastry arm of Alexander's Steakhouse, doing glossy entremets, macarons and a very good croissant on Castro Street. More Tokyo pâtisserie than French bakery — come for something pretty.
items.source: alexanderspatisserie.com; Mountain View Voice; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Mountain View Farmer's Market
items.why: One of the biggest markets on the Peninsula, in the Caltrain station lot every Sunday morning — stone fruit, Asian greens, dumplings and hot food, at the bottom of Castro Street.
items.source: pcfma.org; Mountain View Voice; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Chez TJ
items.why: Tasting-menu French cooking in a Victorian house on Villa Street, a block from Castro, long recognised by the Michelin Guide. The place in Mountain View for an occasion — book ahead.
items.source: Michelin Guide; cheztj.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Udon Mugizo
items.why: Handmade udon — thick, bouncy noodles with tempura or in a mentaiko cream sauce. Small room, quick turnover, a long queue at lunch for good reason.
items.source: Michelin Guide; SF Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Doppio Zero
items.why: Neapolitan pizza from a wood-fired oven, with fresh pasta alongside, on Castro Street. Reliable, warm, and good for a group.
items.source: doppiozeropizza.com; Mountain View Voice; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Kirin
items.why: A Castro Street fixture for decades, now Kirin Chinese Fusion under new owners — Cantonese cooking and dim sum, a big menu and a useful place for a family lunch.
items.source: Mountain View Voice; Yelp; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Oren's Hummus Shop
items.why: Israeli hummus bowls, warm pita and shakshuka. Quick, cheap and very good for a weekday lunch on Castro.
items.source: orenshummus.com; Mountain View Voice; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Din Tai Fung
items.area: Westfield Valley Fair, across Stevens Creek from Santana Row
items.why: The Taiwanese dumpling house, in Valley Fair across the road from Santana Row, and the reason for the queue. Xiao long bao pleated to eighteen folds, the truffle version, and the green beans. Join the virtual waitlist and wander the Row while you wait.
items.source: dintaifungusa.com; San Jose Mercury News; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Tai Er Sichuan Cuisine
items.area: Westfield Valley Fair, across Stevens Creek from Santana Row
items.why: The Chinese chain built on one dish: pickled mustard-green fish in a sour, spicy broth, brought to the table in a basin. Order that, and share.
items.source: San Jose Mercury News; Yelp; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Baekjeong
items.area: Westfield Valley Fair, across Stevens Creek from Santana Row
items.why: Korean barbecue from the K-Town chain — prime cuts grilled at the table with egg and corn-cheese cooked in the rim of the grill. Loud and fun, and best with four people.
items.source: baekjeongusa.com; San Jose Mercury News; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Ox 9 Lan Zhou Handpulled Noodles
items.area: Westfield Valley Fair, across Stevens Creek from Santana Row
items.why: Lanzhou beef noodle soup, the noodles pulled to your chosen thickness as you order. Clear broth, chilli oil, radish — a fast, cheap lunch.
items.source: Yelp; San Jose Mercury News; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Uncle Tetsu
items.area: Westfield Valley Fair, across Stevens Creek from Santana Row
items.why: Japanese cheesecake — jiggly, souffléd, barely sweet — baked in batches all day and sold whole. Eat one warm.
items.source: uncletetsu-us.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Smitten Ice Cream
items.why: Ice cream churned to order with liquid nitrogen, so there is no stabiliser and no freezer case. The salted caramel is the one to try.
items.source: smittenicecream.com; SF Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Salt & Straw
items.why: Portland's small-batch ice cream, with odd, seasonal flavours you can taste before you choose. Expect a queue on a warm evening.
items.source: saltandstraw.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Lady M
items.area: Westfield Valley Fair, across Stevens Creek from Santana Row
items.why: The mille crêpes cake from New York — twenty paper-thin crêpes layered with cream. The green tea slice is the one people come back for.
items.source: ladym.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: SomiSomi
items.why: Soft serve in a fish-shaped taiyaki cone with red bean or custard in the tail. Ube is the flavour.
items.source: somisomi.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Blue Bottle Coffee
items.why: A careful pour-over or a New Orleans iced coffee from the Oakland roaster, in a bright room on the Row. The best coffee within a short walk of Santana Row.
items.source: bluebottlecoffee.com; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Japantown Certified Farmer’s Market
items.why: Sunday mornings on Jackson Street in San José’s Japantown, one of the last three historic Japantowns in the country. Asian produce and hot food, with the neighbourhood’s old mochi shops a block away.
items.source: pcfma.org; San Jose Mercury News; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap
items.hoursNote: Sundays 8 to noon, May to October only.

items.title: Swensen's Ice Cream
items.why: The original Swensen's, on the corner of Union and Hyde since 1948 — a tiny shop on the cable car line with the old-fashioned flavours in the case. Take a cone up the hill.
items.source: SFGate; SF Chronicle; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Satura Cakes
items.why: Japanese-French cakes in downtown Los Altos — light chiffon, strawberry shortcake with barely-sweet cream, and a very good cream puff. Delicate in a way American cakes rarely are.
items.source: saturacakes.com; Los Altos Town Crier; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Tea Era
items.why: A Taiwanese tea bar on Castro Street, brewing loose-leaf oolongs properly as well as milk tea. The place to go when you want tea rather than sugar.

items.title: Seasons Noodle & Dumpling Garden
